title: Route each document to the least risky reader path
description: Choose an input shape and a parse route. The visible output contract changes with text-layer detection, OCR, table analysis, and attachment handling.

profiles.label: Born-digital PDF report
profiles.detail: Copyable text, headings, two-column pages, and bordered tables.

profiles.label: Scanned invoice
profiles.detail: Image-only pages with rotation, fields, and tables that require recognition.

profiles.label: Mixed PDF binder
profiles.detail: Native pages, scanned inserts, inconsistent orientation, and page-level quality changes.

profiles.label: DOCX with attachments
profiles.detail: Native paragraphs, tables, annotations, metadata, and embedded files.

routes.label: Auto-detect PDF text layer
routes.detail: Use auto_tabby, table analysis, automatic orientation, and a tree output.

routes.label: Force image and OCR path
routes.detail: Treat PDF pages as images and pay the recognition cost deliberately.

routes.label: Use native format reader
routes.detail: Preserve native document objects, tables, metadata, and attachments.

routes.label: Fast text-only route
routes.detail: Skip costly table analysis and attachments when the downstream contract permits it.

outcomes.explanation: The route detects and reuses the textual layer, preserves reading order, and enables the faster table path for born-digital pages.
OCR can recover the text but discards a trustworthy native layer and adds avoidable compute and recognition error.
A DOCX-style native reader does not satisfy a PDF input contract. Route by detected format before choosing structure parameters.

outcomes.reader: PDF text path without table analysis
outcomes.explanation: The route is efficient when plain text is the declared output, but it cannot satisfy a table-aware structured contract.
Automatic detection routes the image-only pages to recognition while orientation and table analysis preserve the invoice contract.
The operator knows the pages are scans, so forcing the image path avoids a detection branch and makes the expensive choice explicit.
The input is an image. A route that refuses OCR cannot produce the required text or table structure.
Text may be adequate for search, but row and cell relationships are lost. Do not use it when totals or line items drive decisions.
Page-level detection handles quality changes inside the binder instead of choosing one reader from the first pages only.
The route is robust to scans but needlessly re-recognizes trustworthy native pages and raises tail latency.
Scanned inserts disappear because one native-text decision is applied to a mixed document.
Useful for broad search ingestion, but the flattened output cannot support hierarchy or table-sensitive downstream work.
PDF parameters do not match a DOCX container. Detect the format and select the native reader first.
Rendering and OCR throw away native hierarchy, annotations, attachments, and metadata that the DOCX reader can preserve.
The native reader preserves lines, tables, annotations, metadata, and attached content before structure construction.
Efficient for a text-only index, but attachments and native structural relationships are intentionally excluded.
